4383.t: σάνδαλον (sándalon) + -ιον (-ion, diminutive), of uncertain origin, possibly loaned from Parthian, Persian, or another substrate of Asia Minor.

4375.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pterón, from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂r̥ (“feather”). Related to πέτομαι (pétomai, “I fly”).

4314.t: Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀗𐀪𐀺𐀈 (mo-ri-wo-do), from an Anatolian word cognate with Lydian 𐤪𐤠𐤭𐤦𐤥𐤣𐤠 (mariwda, “dark”), from Proto-Indo-European *morgʷ-iyo-, from a root *mergʷ- (“dark”), whence also English murky and Russian мрак (mrak, “darkness”).

4385.t: Unknown. The cluster /stʰ/ is unusual for Ancient Greek terms inherited from Proto-Indo-European.

4318.t: From Proto-Hellenic *mólā, from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind; crush”). Doublet of μύλος (mŭ́los).

4302.t: Formation like μανδάκης (mandákēs) and καυνάκης (kaunákēs). Usually considered to be a Gaulish word, with cognates in Latin monīle (“necklace, collar”) and Proto-Germanic *manją (“collar”).

4303.t: Uncertain. One proposed etymology maintains that the verb derived from Proto-Indo-European *mr̥n̥-ye-ti, a denominative in *-yeti to a nasal-infixed form of the root Proto-Indo-European *mer- (“to die”).

4397.t: From Proto-Hellenic *stōyyā́, from Proto-Indo-European *stoh₂-w-ih₂, ultimately from the root *steh₂- (“to stand”), whence also στῦλος (stûlos, “column, pillar”).

4378.t: A nominalization of the verb πήγνυμι (pḗgnumi, “to stick, fasten, build, fix”), meaning "that what is built or fixed"; see also πάγη (págē, “snare, trap”) and Latin pagus.

4399.t: From στέλλω (stéllō, “to send”) + -ος (-os). See also στολή (stolḗ).

4364.t: From προδίδωμι (prodídōmi, “to betray”) + -της (-tēs, masculine agent-noun suffix).

4315.t: Perhaps from Pre-Greek. Compare also μάχαιρα (mákhaira, “large sword”).

4380.t: Uncertain: Compare Sanskrit परशु (paraśú, “axe”) and Ossetian фӕрӕт (færæt, “axe”), pointing to a late, dialectal Proto-Indo-European word like *peleḱu- which does not appear to be a native formation.

4369.t: From προσέχω (prosékhō, “to guard against”) + -η (-ē, abstract noun suffix).

4394.t: According to Beekes, a Proto-Indo-European *th₂eys- (“dough”), whence also Proto-Slavic *těsto (“dough”), Old Irish táis (“dough”), and Old English þǣsma (“leaven”), with an influence from στέαρ (stéar, “fat”).

4322.t: Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *neyk- (“to attack, start vehemently”), cognate with Lithuanian ap-ni̇̀kti (“to attack”), su-ni̇̀kti (“to attack”), Latvian nikns (“bad, grim, vehement”), Albanian nis, and possibly Russian в-никнуть (v-niknutʹ),…

4331.t: From Proto-Indo-European *ksu-ró-s (“razor”), from *ksew- (“to scrape, sharpen, shave”). Exact cognate with Proto-Indo-Iranian *kšurás (“dagger, razor”); see also the verbal formation from the same root ξύω (xúō, “to scrape”).

4306.t: Uncertain; possibly from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to measure”) or *med- (“to be full”), the latter comparable to Sanskrit मत्त (mattá, “drunk, intoxicated”).

4391.t: Uncertain. Often derived from σκάλλω (skállō, “to stir, hoe”) or from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelh₃p-, from *(s)kelh₃- (“to cut”), and so related to Latin scalpō (“to scratch”), English shelf and Lithuanian sklempti (“to plane”).

4384.t: The formation is common to other technical terms like δοκίς (dokís, “beam”), ἀρίς (arís, “bow-drill”) and σελίς (selís, “crossbeam”) but the origin is uncertain.

4316.t: Explained by the ancients as deriving from μέλας (mélas, “black”), because of the soot which accumulates on the ceiling.

4332.t: From the root of ξύω (xúō, “to scrape, plane”) + -τός (-tós, adjectival suffix).

4336.t: From Proto-Hellenic *eworhéyō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁wors-éye-ti (“to make it rain”), from *h₁wers-.

4356.t: From περι- (peri-, “around”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “to make ready, to prepare”).

4320.t: From the same root as νεῦρον (neûron).

4342.t: παν- (pan-) + ἄγυρις (águris), Aeolic form of ἀγορά (ăgorā́, “marketplace”)

4392.t: From σμήχω (smḗkhō, “to wipe; to soap off”) + -μα (-mă).

4328.t: Related to νύξ (núx, “night”). Beekes compares the suffix to one in Latin nocturnus.

4366.t: From προμάχομαι (promákhomai, “to fight in front”), from προ- (pro-) + μάχομαι (mákhomai, “to fight, do battle”); closely related to πρόμαχος (prómakhos).
